narration: The World on One Floor
This is international folk dance. 20th century to present.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The movement developed in early 20th-century U.S. immigrant communities.
Vytautas Beliajus is credited as a primary founder in the 1930s.
Song Chang, a Chinese illustrator, pioneered Scandinavian dancing for non-Scandinavians in San Francisco.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The primary occasion is recreational enjoyment and the preservation of folk arts.
It serves as a tool for cultural exchange and community building.
In the case of Israeli dance, it was used to help build a common national culture from multiple immigrant communities.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: 42nd Annual International Folk Dance Festival at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion (https://archive.org/details/calauem_000210)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is typically performed in a club setting, often requiring no previous experience or partner.
Formations vary by the specific ethnic genre being performed, but often include circles, lines, and partner sets like those found in contra or English country dance.
Classes involve a master teacher demonstrating steps which are then added to a group's repertoire.
Watch for Grapevine, Yemenite Step.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Primarily communal circles and lines moving counter-clockwise (LOD).
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is as diverse as the dance repertoire, featuring Balkan brass, Middle Eastern percussion, Scandinavian fiddles, and Israeli accordion music.
Historically, live music was common, such as the accordion players at Detroit JCC groups, but modern clubs often use recorded playlists.
Listen for the Accordion, Fiddle, Clarinet, Gaida.
The pulse is Variable at about 110 beats a minute.

A shifting soundscape that moves between the bright, accordion-heavy sounds of Israeli dance, the complex odd-metered brass and woodwinds of the Balkans, and the driving fiddle tunes of Northern Europe.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Live performances — Orkestar Bez Ime
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Varies from steady polkas to additive Balkan rhythms.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Settings range from university gyms and street closures—such as Detroit's Second Avenue—to dedicated venues like Ashkenaz in Berkeley.
While recreational dancing is done in casual attire, performing groups like the Aman Folk Ensemble use authentic ethnic costumes.
Festivals and camps often provide a 'village' atmosphere where dancers sleep and eat on-site.
on_screen: Image gallery: 1 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key pioneers include Vytautas Beliajus, Song Chang, Michael and Mary Ann Herman, Jane Farwell, and Dick Crum.
Later influential figures include Athan Karras and Rudy Dannes (founders of The Intersection), Dani Dassa (Cafe Danssa), and David Nadel (Ashkenaz).
While the 'international' style is a U.S. construct, it has spread to Japan, Australia, and Europe.
It is a subclass of folk dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: international folk dance is influence of Israeli folk dance: A major component of the international repertoire since the 1950s.
international folk dance is influence of Balkan dance: One of the most popular genres within international folk dance clubs.
international folk dance is sibling of Contra dance: Often shared in the same club settings and festivals.
